generated_note: Generated from production by scripts/build-finder-harness-fixture.ts. Real rows, chosen to cover the cases the acceptance run has to exercise. Do not hand-edit — regenerate.

drills.description: Two lines on the ground — chalk, tape, or a pair of bats laid down — marking where the front foot starts and where it should land. The hitter takes normal swings off a tee or front toss and the only rule is that the front foot lands inside the box. A stride that drifts open, closes off, or grows by six inches when the hitter tries to do more is invisible to them and obvious the moment there is a line to miss.
equipment_needed: chalk, tape or two spare bats
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "same foot, same spot, every swing". Watch the BACK foot as well: a hitter who cannot keep the stride in the box usually has the back side collapsing first, and fixing the front foot alone will not hold. A front foot landing outside the box toward the plate is diving; outside away from it is bailing. Same miss, two different problems.
success_markers: Front foot lands inside the box on eight of ten swings
The tenth stride looks like the first
The hitter notices a miss before the coach mentions it
drills.regression_notes: Drop to one line, for the landing spot only, and let the hitter stride to it at their own pace with no ball involved.
drills.progression_notes: Move from tee to front toss, then have the feeder vary the timing — a late toss is what makes a stride grow.

drills.drill_name: Crow Hop — Arm Strength and Outfield Throwing
drills.description: The footwork an outfielder uses to put their whole body behind a long throw. After catching the ball the player hops onto the throwing-side foot, plants it, strides forward with the front foot, and throws — hop, plant, stride, throw. It converts a standing throw into a moving one, and for a player who has only ever thrown flat-footed it adds more distance in one session than a month of arm strength work.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: The crow hop is like winding up a throw with your whole body. After you catch the ball: hop onto your throwing-side foot, then stride forward with your front foot and throw. Hop, stride, throw! You will throw much harder when your whole body moves toward the target. Practice from short distance first, then go longer.
success_markers: Hop lands on the throwing-side foot, not the front foot
Body is moving toward the target at release rather than stopping to throw
Throw carries noticeably further than the same player's flat-footed throw
drills.regression_notes: Walk through hop-plant-stride with no ball, then add a short throw. The sequence is the hard part; the distance takes care of itself once the feet are right.
drills.progression_notes: Add distance, then catch a thrown ball or a fly ball first so the hop starts from a real play rather than from a standstill.

drills.drill_name: The Catch Drill — Track & Read Pitches
drills.description: Pitch recognition with the swing removed. The hitter stands in the box wearing a helmet, holding a glove instead of a bat, and catches the pitch — calling 'fastball' or 'change' as early as they can read it. Correct early calls score. Because there is no swing to get wrong, all the attention goes to the ball out of the hand, and it can be run free during a pitcher's bullpen by rotating hitters through the box.
drills.safety_notes: Helmet required when standing in the box; start with reduced-speed pitching for younger hitters.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Hitter stands in the box wearing a helmet with a glove and catches the pitch, calling 'fastball' or 'change' as early as possible. Score correct early calls. Rotate hitters standing in during bullpens for free reps.
success_markers: Calls pitch type before the ball is halfway home
Correctly takes balls and 'catches strikes' by location call
Carries calmer takes into live at-bats
drills.regression_notes: Slow the pitching down, or drop to calling 'strike' and 'ball' instead of pitch type. Location is easier to read than spin and still worth training.
drills.progression_notes: Add a third pitch type, require the call earlier, or put a bat back in their hands with a take-only rule so the recognition has to survive the urge to swing.

drills.description: Bunting practice with a scoreboard. Split the team in two. Each hitter draws a situation — sacrifice to third, push past the pitcher, squeeze — and gets one attempt against live pitching or a machine. Points only for a bunt that actually executes the situation drawn; a good bunt to the wrong side scores nothing. Four to six attempts each, and the losing team clears the field. Bunting is the skill most likely to be practised without pressure and then attempted under maximum pressure, which is the gap this closes.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: The situation card is what makes this work — the hitter has to pick the bunt type themselves rather than being told. Do not coach mid-attempt; let the failed ones fail and talk afterwards. Live pitching matters here more than anywhere else in the bunting category, because bunting a machine ball is a different skill from bunting a teammate's.
success_markers: Executes 3 different bunt types against live pitching
Success rate climbs across sessions
Players choose the right bunt for the situation without coaching
drills.regression_notes: Drop to one bunt type per round and toss instead of pitching. The competition still works, and the decision can be added once the technique holds up.
drills.progression_notes: Add a runner so the bunt has a real consequence, tighten the target areas, or make an unexecuted bunt cost a point rather than simply scoring none.

drills.description: The Albert Pujols drill — hitters drop to one knee in their launch position and work purely on upper-body rotation and hand path to the ball. Eliminates lower body mechanics so players can isolate and feel proper hand/shoulder action.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Get down on your back knee. From this position it's all about your hands and rotation. Drive your top hand through the ball — aim for backspin line drives to the opposite field gap. Feel your shoulders rotating, not just your arms.
success_markers: Rotation comes from the core and hips rather than the arms
Balance holds on the knees through the finish
Contact quality holds up despite the lower body being removed
drills.regression_notes: Kneel on a mat or soft grass and swing at half speed, or swing dry with no ball. Kneeling is uncomfortable enough to distract a young hitter from the movement.
drills.progression_notes: Stand up and take the same rotation into a normal swing in the same round, so the feel carries before it fades.

drills.description: A dry swing that stops at full extension and holds there. The hitter swings at half speed and freezes the moment the arms are fully extended out in front — before the wrists roll over and the bat wraps around the body. Held for a count of three, it shows both coach and hitter exactly where the barrel and hands finish, which is a position most young hitters swing through without ever feeling.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Half speed, or the freeze is impossible. Look for both arms extended and the barrel still out in front of the body, not wrapped behind the shoulder. If they cannot hold it without falling forward, the swing is going around them rather than through the ball. Do a few with a ball on a tee afterwards so the position connects to actual contact.
success_markers: Holds the extended position for three seconds without losing balance
Both arms extended with the barrel in front of the body, not wrapped
Can find the position without the coach placing them in it
drills.regression_notes: Place them into the extension position by hand and let them feel it before trying to swing into it. Working backwards from the finish is easier than finding it from the start.
drills.progression_notes: Speed the swing up while keeping the finish, then hit off a tee and freeze after contact. The position has to survive a real swing to be worth anything.

drills.description: Hitters use only their bottom hand to swing at a ball on the tee. This drill isolates the lead arm and trains the knob to ball path — the direct, short path the hands should take toward the baseball.
equipment_needed: one-hand training bat or short bat
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Hold the bat with just your bottom hand. Think knob to ball — pull the knob of the bat directly toward the ball as fast as you can. This one is harder because it's usually your weaker hand. Keep your elbow close to your body as you start the swing.
success_markers: Knob leads toward the ball rather than the barrel casting out first
Front elbow stays close to the body at the start of the swing
Makes solid contact off the tee without the barrel dropping under the ball
drills.regression_notes: Choke right up on a light or shortened bat and take half-speed swings. The lead arm is usually the weaker one, and a heavy bat turns this into a slinging drill.
drills.progression_notes: Switch to the top-hand version, then put both hands back on and check whether the shorter path survives. Alternating one-hand and two-hand sets within a round transfers it fastest.

drills.description: Each hand's job in the swing, isolated by taking the other one off the bat. The hitter uses a lighter or shorter bat and hits off a tee with the bottom hand only for a set, then the top hand only for a set. The bottom hand learns to pull the knob toward the ball; the top hand learns to drive through it with the palm facing up. Neither can hide behind the other, which is the point.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: A lighter bat is not optional — a full-size bat one-handed teaches a young hitter to sling it. Bottom hand: knob to the ball, elbow close. Top hand: palm up through contact, push it forward. The thing to watch for in both is the body stopping and the arm taking over; the rotation still has to happen, and a hitter who is arm-swinging will be visibly still from the waist down.
success_markers: Bottom-hand swings pull the knob at the ball rather than casting the barrel out
Top-hand swings finish with the palm up and the ball driven, not slapped
Body rotates on both versions — no pure arm swings
drills.regression_notes: Choke right up on a light bat and take slow half swings, or swing with no ball at all until the feel is there. One-handed hitting is genuinely hard for an eight-year-old and a heavy bat makes it pointless.
drills.progression_notes: Put both hands back on and see whether the path survives. Alternate a one-hand set with a two-hand set so the transfer happens in the same session.

drills.description: Hitters use only their top hand to swing at a ball on the tee. The top hand's job is to drive through the ball with the palm facing up at contact. This drill builds top-hand strength and teaches proper bat-path extension.
equipment_needed: one-hand training bat or short bat
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Hold the bat with just your top hand. Drive through the ball like you're hitting it with your palm facing up — like you're serving a pizza! Finish with your hand high. If the ball goes weak to the pull side, your hand is rolling over too early.
drills.reps_guidance: 2 sets of 8 with a light bat
success_markers: Palm stays up through contact rather than rolling over early
Ball is driven off the tee rather than slapped or pushed
Body still rotates — the swing is not purely the arm
drills.regression_notes: Use a light or shortened bat and swing at half speed. If the barrel is dropping, the bat is too heavy for one hand at this age.
drills.progression_notes: Alternate with the bottom-hand version, then put both hands back on within the same round so the feel transfers while it is fresh.

drills.description: The hitter stands in with a helmet on. The coach kneels behind an L-screen about twenty feet away with a bucket of soft-core balls and says "turn" before throwing one at the hitter's back hip. The hitter turns the front shoulder in, tucks the chin, drops the hands and takes it on the back. Ten of those. Then ten pitches over the plate, mixed in unannounced, so the hitter has to read which is which. Fear at the plate is almost always fear of being hit, and a hitter who has been hit twenty times with a soft ball and found out it is survivable stops guessing about it.
drills.safety_notes: SOFT-CORE BALLS ONLY, helmet on, and nothing thrown above the shoulders. Never run this with a real baseball. Stop immediately if a player is distressed — a frightened player getting more reps is not learning, and this drill exists to remove fear rather than to prove a point about it.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "turn in, never away" and "chin to the chest". The instinct being replaced is turning the FRONT of the body toward the ball, which exposes the face and the hands — a hitter doing that is more at risk, not less, and it is the one thing worth stopping the drill for. If they bail on the pitches over the plate, go back to announced reps: that means the fear is still ahead of the practice, and more unannounced reps will only confirm it.
success_markers: Turns the front shoulder in rather than away
Takes it on the back or the rear, never on the hands
Stays in the box on the pitches over the plate
drills.regression_notes: No throw at all. The coach says "turn" and the hitter rehearses it on an empty box, ten times, until the shoulder goes the right way without thinking. Then add the ball.
drills.progression_notes: Front toss with a soft ball, unannounced, mixed in with strikes that are there to be hit — so the hitter is deciding between swinging and turning rather than only ever turning.

drills.description: The feeder stands beside the hitter and slightly in front, holds a ball at about shoulder height on an outstretched arm, and simply lets go. The hitter has to get the barrel there before it lands. No toss, no arc, nothing to read but the release. It is the shortest possible gap between now and swing, which is why it finds a long or slow path faster than any tee can.
drills.safety_notes: The feeder's hand and forearm are near the swing path. Stand beside and slightly in front of the hitter, never in front of the plate, release and withdraw in one motion, and keep a helmet on the hitter. Start slow enough that the feeder is never guessing when the swing is coming.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "short to it". The failure is almost never reaction time — it is path length, and a hitter who keeps missing is going around the ball rather than to it. When they need more time, drop from LOWER. Dropping closer to the hitter gives them no more time and puts the feeder's hand in the swing.
success_markers: Barrel meets the ball above knee height
Contact happens out front, not beside the back foot
Six clean of ten
drills.regression_notes: Drop from waist height so the ball has further to fall and the hitter has longer to find it.
drills.progression_notes: Drop from higher, then hold two balls and release one — the hitter reads which.

drills.description: What staying back actually means, drilled against pitches that punish not doing it. A feeder throws front toss and varies fast and slow without telling the hitter which is coming. The stride still lands on time for a fastball — that part does not change — but the hands wait. Three rounds of twelve mixed-speed swings. A hitter who solves this by striding late has not learned to stay back; they have learned to be late on everything.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Front toss with random speed changes: the feeder varies fast/slow without telling. Cue 'stride to hit the fastball, keep the hands back for the change.' The stride lands on time — the hands wait.
success_markers: Head and weight stay behind the front hip on slow pitches
Hard contact on both speeds within the same round
No double-stride or lunge when fooled
drills.regression_notes: Announce the speed before each toss so the adjustment can be practised deliberately, then stop announcing. Bounce toss is a gentler introduction to an unpredictable ball path.
drills.progression_notes: Widen the speed gap, add a third speed, or move to live pitching with a pitcher who genuinely has an off-speed pitch.

drills.description: The coach deliberately rolls balls that cannot be fielded cleanly — off to the side, off the heel of the glove, a short hop that eats the fielder up. The rep does not end at the bobble. The fielder finds the ball, picks it barehanded if that is quicker, and still makes the throw. Youth infielders practise clean ground balls almost exclusively and then meet their first bad hop in a game, where the ball on the ground is not the error. Standing and looking at it is.
common_flaws_fixed: rushes the throw after a mistake
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "find it, then go". The clock a fielder imagines after a bobble is always shorter than the real one — on most youth fields there is still time to get the out, and believing that is most of the drill. Watch for the head dropping and the shoulders following it: a player who has already got annoyed has stopped playing, and that is the habit worth interrupting rather than the bobble.
success_markers: Moves to the loose ball rather than reaching for it
Barehands it when the ball has stopped
Completes the throw on more than half the bad reps
drills.regression_notes: Roll only slightly off-line so the ball can still be fielded, and ask for a clean pick-up with no throw at all.
drills.progression_notes: Add a runner, or a stopwatch, so the throw has to beat something real.

drills.description: A rotating team circuit with a different baserunning skill at each base. At home, an explosive three-step start on a coach's signal. At first, a lead and a break toward second. At second, reading a coach's point to advance or hold. At third, a read on a ball in the dirt. Players move around the circuit in small groups so everyone is working at once, and the whole thing doubles as conditioning without ever looking like conditioning.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: The first three steps are where baserunning is won or lost, so make the start signal unpredictable at every station. 'Eyes on the coach, not on your feet' — a runner watching the ground cannot take the extra base. Keep groups small and the rotation brisk. Timing the stations gives them something to chase and stops the circuit drifting into a walk.
success_markers: First three steps are explosive rather than a gradual build
Runners look up to find the coach rather than watching their feet
Turns cut the inside corner of the base instead of swinging wide
drills.regression_notes: Two stations instead of four, and remove the reads so it is pure starts and turns. Four decisions at four bases is too much for a first session.
drills.progression_notes: Add live reads at every station, put a clock on the circuit, or run two groups against each other for a team score.

drills.description: A ground ball to the right side pulls the first baseman off the bag and somebody has to be there. The coach hits or rolls to first, the first baseman fields it, and the pitcher breaks for the bag on contact — every time, including the times the first baseman stays home and takes it themselves. The feed is a soft underhand toss led in front of the pitcher, chest high, to a spot they are running to.
drills.safety_notes: The pitcher and the runner arrive at the same base from different directions. Run the bag on the foul side and past it, and do not add a live runner until the footwork is automatic.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "break on contact, not on the bobble". The standard youth version is the pitcher watching the play develop and arriving late, and the fix is making the break automatic rather than conditional. The feed goes where the pitcher WILL be: a toss aimed at where they are is behind them by the time it arrives. Catch first, then find the bag — a pitcher hunting for the base with the ball still in the air misses both.
success_markers: Pitcher moves on contact without being told
Catches the feed before touching the bag
Runs through toward the infield rather than stopping on the bag
drills.regression_notes: Walk it through with no ball, then at half speed, so the path and the timing are learned before the catch is added.
drills.progression_notes: Mix in balls the first baseman can take unassisted, so the pitcher breaks every time and gets waved off some of them.

drills.description: The coach starts the outfielder moving before the ball is in the air — a jog left, right, or straight in — and then throws or hits a ball that has to be caught while they are still moving. Nothing is hit to where the player is standing. Almost all youth outfield practice is a ball sent to a stationary player, and almost no ball in a game arrives that way.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "run first, glove last". A glove that comes up on the first step slows the player down and costs more ground than it saves. Watch the route rather than the catch: a player drifting in a curve is reading late, and the thing to fix is the first step, not the speed.
success_markers: Glove comes up in the last two strides, not the first
Runs a straight line to the spot
Two hands when there is time, one when there is not
drills.regression_notes: Start the player moving and throw the ball to where they already are, so the movement is the only new thing.
drills.progression_notes: Stop calling the direction and let them read it off the coach's swing.

drills.description: The fielder stands fifteen feet from the coach with a bucket of soft-core balls between them. The coach tosses underhand so the ball peaks about ten feet up and comes down into the glove. Catch it, toss it back, go again. Every three clean catches the fielder takes one step back; a drop or a flinch moves them one step forward, not back to the start. The distance is the whole drill. A player who flinches under a fly ball is not short of technique — they are short of reps that ended well, and the ladder is how those get built without anyone being asked to be brave.
mechanic_focus: tracking a ball in the air
drills.safety_notes: Soft-core or tennis balls only until the player is catching cleanly at thirty feet. Putting a real baseball on a fearful player undoes the whole progression, and one bad one costs more ground than ten good ones gain.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "thumbs together, watch it into the glove". The flinch to watch for is the head turning away in the last foot, and it happens before the hands do anything wrong — correcting the hands will not fix it. Move closer until the head stays still, then start climbing again. Never move a player back because the rest of the group moved back; the ladder is per player and that is the point of it.
drills.reps_guidance: 8-10 minutes; three clean catches buys one step back
success_markers: Eyes stay on the ball all the way into the glove
Catches above the head rather than trapping it at the chest
Takes a step back without being asked to
drills.regression_notes: Sit the fielder on a bucket so they cannot back away, and toss from eight feet. Almost every player catches from there, and one clean catch is the thing worth building on.
drills.progression_notes: Swap the soft ball for a baseball at the SAME distance before adding any more distance — change one variable at a time. Then move the coach back to forty feet with a fungo, so the ball arrives off a bat rather than out of a hand.

drills.description: A full swing off a tee or front toss, and then the hitter runs — properly, all the way through the base, every single time. No jogging, no watching the ball, no eighty percent. The bat is placed down rather than thrown. Youth players take hundreds of swings a week and attach running to almost none of them, so in a game the first three steps out of the box are the steps they have never practised.
drills.safety_notes: The bat goes down in a designated spot, never thrown. Nobody stands on the first-base line while a hitter is running.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "drop it and go". The tell is a hitter who watches the ball before moving: on a youth field a batted ball is nearly always still in play, and that half-second is the whole difference between safe and out. Run THROUGH the base rather than to it — a player who slows down two steps early has turned a close play into an out without knowing it.
drills.reps_guidance: 10 swings, each with a full run
success_markers: First step is toward first, not back toward the plate
Bat placed down, clear of the path
Runs past the bag without slowing
drills.regression_notes: Split it — swing, freeze, then run on a whistle — so the two halves join at the player's own pace.
drills.progression_notes: The coach calls "fair" or "foul" as the ball leaves, and the runner reacts to it.

drills.description: The runner starts in the box and the coach points — or rolls a ball — to the infield or the outfield just after the imaginary swing. Ball on the ground in the infield: run through the bag. Ball through to the outfield: round it hard and look. Same start, two answers, and the runner has to pick one while already moving. Most young runners have exactly one setting, and it is usually the wrong one for whichever ball just happened.
drills.primary_skill: reading the ball out of the box
mechanic_focus: reading the ball out of the box
common_flaws_fixed: watches the coach instead of the ball
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "through it or around it — decide before the bag, not on it". A runner who rounds everything gives away outs at first; one who runs through everything gives away second on a ball in the gap. Watch the path: a proper round starts with a small arc three steps BEFORE the bag, not a hard left turn on top of it.
success_markers: Arcs out early on a ball to the outfield
Runs straight through on an infield ground ball
Looks at the ball rather than at the coach
drills.regression_notes: Announce the answer before the start, so the running is practised before the deciding is added.
drills.progression_notes: A live fungo instead of a pointed direction, so the read comes off a real ball.

drills.description: A runner on a base, a coach with a ball, and a fielder to catch it. The coach throws a fly ball; the runner goes back to the base, watches the catch, and leaves on the catch — not before it, not a beat after. Three rounds: first the runner is told to tag, then told only that a ball is in the air, then given a mix of fly balls, line drives and ground balls so that tagging becomes a decision rather than an instruction.
drills.secondary_skill: reading a ball in the air
mechanic_focus: reading a ball in the air
common_flaws_fixed: watches the fielder instead of the ball
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "leave on the catch, not on the throw". The universal youth error is watching the fielder's arm instead of their glove; move the runner's eyes to the catch itself and the timing fixes itself. On a line drive the right answer is to freeze, and the third round is the only place that ever gets practised.
success_markers: Foot stays on the base until the ball is caught
Leaves within a stride of the catch
Freezes on a line drive without being told
drills.regression_notes: Stand beside the runner and say "now" at the moment of the catch, until the timing is felt rather than counted.
drills.progression_notes: Add a second runner so they have to communicate, and a throw so the tag has to beat something.

drills.description: Bunting practice where placement is scored, not just contact. Lay towels or cone lanes down the first-base and third-base lines, a few feet from the plate. A feeder tosses from short range and calls 'first' or 'third' as the ball is released, and the hitter has to deaden the ball and steer it into the called lane. Ten bunts a round, alternating. It is the drill that turns a player who can bunt into a player who can bunt somewhere.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Call the side late — as the ball leaves your hand — or the hitter sets the bat angle in advance and learns nothing. 'Catch it with the barrel' gives you the soft top hand that deadens the ball. The knob chases the angle, not the barrel: the hitter steers by turning the bat around the top hand, not by pushing the end of it.
drills.reps_guidance: 3 rounds of 10 bunts, alternating target lanes
success_markers: 7+ of 10 bunts stop inside the called lane
Ball dies within 15 feet of the plate
Bat starts at the top of the zone — anything above it is taken
drills.regression_notes: Call the side before the toss, or bunt from a tee into the lanes with no feeder at all. Separating the placement from the reaction makes both learnable.
drills.progression_notes: Move to live pitching, shrink the lanes, or add a take rule so the hitter has to judge the pitch as well as place the bunt.

drills.description: A runner on base, a catcher or a coach behind the plate, and a ball thrown deliberately into the dirt. The runner reads whether it got past the catcher and goes or stays on that read alone. Some of them are blocked and stay in front, and those are the ones worth practising — the runner who goes on every ball in the dirt is out by fifteen feet, and the one who never goes never takes the base.
drills.primary_skill: reading a ball in the dirt
mechanic_focus: reading a ball in the dirt
common_flaws_fixed: never advances on a wild pitch
goes on every ball in the dirt
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Cue "read the ball, not the catcher". A ball that stays in front of the catcher is not a wild pitch, and a runner watching the catcher's body instead of the ball cannot tell the difference. Secondary lead first: a runner still standing on the bag when the ball hits the dirt has already lost the base, whatever they do next.
drills.reps_guidance: 10 pitches, roughly half of them blocked
success_markers: Takes a secondary lead on every pitch
Goes only when the ball actually gets past
Commits fully once committed
drills.regression_notes: The coach calls "go" or "stay" as the ball lands, so the running is practised before the reading is added.
drills.progression_notes: A real catcher blocking at game speed, and a throw down, so the read has to be right AND early.

drills.drill_name: Shoulder Swings — Stay Short to the Ball
drills.description: Without a ball, players swing keeping their back elbow tucked into their hip slot as they initiate the swing. The drill creates the sensation of a short, quick path to the hitting zone and eliminates the long, loop cast most youth hitters develop.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Start in your stance. Begin your swing — but keep your back elbow tucked tight to your side. Don't let it fly out. This is what staying short feels like. Do 20 slow motion swings focusing only on that back elbow staying close. Then add speed.
success_markers: Back elbow stays tucked to the side through the start of the swing
Hands get to the zone before the barrel does
Swing visibly shortens across the twenty slow repetitions
drills.regression_notes: Have them hold the tucked position and move only a few inches, or place a glove under the back arm to hold it there. Feeling the position matters more than completing a swing.
drills.progression_notes: Add speed, then add a tee, then soft toss. The elbow slot is the thing to keep checking — it is the first thing to go once a ball is involved.

drills.drill_name: The Rocker Drill — Hip Lead & Weight Shift
drills.description: The hip lead, taught with a rocking start that makes it easy to feel. The pitcher rocks their weight back onto the back foot, then drives the front hip toward home plate while the shoulders stay back and tilted slightly uphill. The arm follows rather than leads. It is the single most useful mechanical correction for a youth pitcher losing both velocity and command, because a shoulder that arrives before the hip has spent the energy before the arm can use it.
drills.ai_coaching_notes: Rock back on your back foot... now drive your HIP toward home plate — not your shoulder! Your hip goes first, your arm follows. Feel like your shoulders are tilting uphill as you stride. If your shoulder gets to home plate before your hip does, you've leaked your energy and lost command.
success_markers: Front hip moves toward the plate before the front shoulder does
Shoulders stay tilted uphill through the stride rather than flattening
Weight stays back on the rock rather than drifting forward with it
drills.regression_notes: Rock and hold without throwing, so the separated position can be felt and checked. A coach standing side-on can show them where the hip is relative to the shoulder.
drills.progression_notes: Remove the rock so the hip lead happens from a normal leg lift, then throw at full effort to a catcher. Pair it with the Square Hips drill for the separation it creates.
